<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a ring. A left $R$-module is an additive abelian group $A$ together with a map
\[
R\times A\to A
\]
such that for all $a,b\in A$ and $r,s\in R$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item $r(a+b)=ra+rb$,
\item $(r+s)a=ra+sa$,
\item $(rs)a=r(sa)$,
\item $1a=a$.
\end{enumerate}
The definition of a right $R$-module is analogous.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $S$ be another ring. An $R$--$S$-bimodule ${}_RA_S$ is an abelian group $A$ that is simultaneously a left $R$-module ${}_RA$ and a right $S$-module $A_S$, and such that for all $a\in A$, $r\in R$, $s\in S$,
\[
(ra)s=r(as).
\]
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a ring. An element $v\in R$ is called \emph{invertible} if there exists an element $x\in R$ such that
\[
vx=1=xv.
\]
Such an $x$ is called the inverse of $v$ and is denoted by $v^{-1}$. Thus
\[
vv^{-1}=1=v^{-1}v.
\]
The element $v^{-1}$ is unique for $v$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
An element $v$ of a ring $R$ is called an \emph{involution} if
\[
v^2=1,
\]
i.e. $v^{-1}=v$. Equivalently, $v$ is an invertible element of order $2$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
Let $K$ be the ring of upper triangular matrices
\[
K=\begin{pmatrix}R&M\\0&S\end{pmatrix},
\]
where $R$ and $S$ have the involution property. A matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
\]
is an involution if and only if $r$ and $s$ are involutions and
\[
rm=-ms.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\emph{Necessity.} Suppose
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
\]
is an involution. This means that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}^{2}
=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Compute
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}r^2&rm+ms\\0&s^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since the original matrix is an involution,
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r^2&rm+ms\\0&s^2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
r^2=1,\qquad s^2=1,\qquad rm+ms=0.
\]
Thus $r$ and $s$ are involutions and $rm=-ms$.

\emph{Sufficiency.} Suppose $r$ and $s$ are involutions and $rm=-ms$. Then
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}r^2&rm+ms\\0&s^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Using $r^2=1$, $s^2=1$, and $rm=-ms$, we obtain
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r^2&rm+ms\\0&s^2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore the matrix is an involution.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
Let
\[
K=\begin{pmatrix}R&M\\0&S\end{pmatrix}
\]
be the ring of upper triangular matrices of order two. Then $K$ has the involution property if and only if $R$ and $S$ have the involution property.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\emph{Necessity.} Suppose that $K$ has the involution property. Take any $r\in R$. It can be written as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}u_1&m_1\\0&u_2\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}v_1&m_2\\0&v_2\end{pmatrix},
\]
where the first matrix is invertible and the second is an involution. Hence $u_1$ is invertible and $v_1$ is an involution (by the preceding lemma). Furthermore,
\[
r=u_1+v_1.
\]
Thus $R$ has the involution property. The proof for $S$ is analogous.

\emph{Sufficiency.} Suppose that $R$ and $S$ have the involution property. Take an arbitrary matrix in the formal matrix ring $K$:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}\in K.
\]
By assumption, the elements $r$ and $s$ can be represented as
\[
r=u_1+v_1,
\qquad
s=u_2+v_2,
\]
where $u_1,u_2$ are invertible and $v_1,v_2$ are involutions.
Then
\[
\begin{pmatrix}r&m\\0&s\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}u_1+v_1&m\\0&u_2+v_2\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}u_1&m\\0&u_2\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}v_1&0\\0&v_2\end{pmatrix},
\]
where
\[
\begin{pmatrix}u_1&m\\0&u_2\end{pmatrix}
\]
is invertible, while
\[
\begin{pmatrix}v_1&0\\0&v_2\end{pmatrix}
\]
is an involution. Therefore $K$ has the involution property.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a formal matrix ring of order $n$,
\[
K=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_1 & M_{1,2} & \cdots & M_{1,n}\\
M_{2,1} & R_2 & \cdots & M_{2,n}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
M_{n,1} & M_{n,2} & \cdots & R_n
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where $R_i$ $(i=1,\ldots,n)$ are rings. If the rings $R_i$ have the involution property, then $K$ also has the involution property.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Take an arbitrary matrix $M$ in the formal matrix ring $K$:
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
r_1 & m_{1,2} & \cdots & m_{1,n}\\
m_{2,1} & r_2 & \cdots & m_{2,n}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
m_{n,1} & m_{n,2} & \cdots & r_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since, by hypothesis, all rings $R_i$ have the involution property, the elements $r_i\in R_i$ $(i=1,\ldots,n)$ can be represented as
\[
r_i=u_i+v_i,
\]
where $u_i$ is invertible and $v_i$ is an involution in $R_i$.

Hence the original matrix $M$ can be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
M
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
u_1+v_1 & m_{1,2} & \cdots & m_{1,n}\\
m_{2,1} & u_2+v_2 & \cdots & m_{2,n}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
m_{n,1} & m_{n,2} & \cdots & u_n+v_n
\end{pmatrix}\\[1ex]
&=
\begin{pmatrix}
u_1 & m_{1,2} & \cdots & m_{1,n}\\
m_{2,1} & u_2 & \cdots & m_{2,n}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
m_{n,1} & m_{n,2} & \cdots & u_n
\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}
v_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\
0 & v_2 & \cdots & 0\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
0 & 0 & \cdots & v_n
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]

We prove by mathematical induction that the formal matrix ring $K$ has the involution property.

Let $n=1$. In this case, the matrix $M$ consists of a single element $r_1$, which has the involution property. Hence it is clear that the formal matrix ring $K$ also has this property.

Now assume $n\ge 2$. Write the original matrix $M$ in block form:
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here $A$ is an $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix,
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_1 & M_{1,2} & \cdots & M_{1,n-1}\\
M_{2,1} & R_2 & \cdots & M_{2,n-1}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
M_{n-1,1} & M_{n-1,2} & \cdots & R_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix},
\]
$C$ is a row vector of size $1\times(n-1)$,
\[
C=(M_{n,1}\; M_{n,2}\; \cdots\; M_{n,n-1}),
\]
$B$ is a column vector of size $(n-1)\times1$,
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}M_{1,n}\\M_{2,n}\\\vdots\\M_{n-1,n}\end{pmatrix},
\]
and $d$ is an element with the involution property, $d\in R_n$.

By the induction hypothesis, the matrix $A$ can be represented as the sum of two matrices,
\[
A=D+U,
\]
where $U$ is invertible and $D$ is a diagonal involution. Put
\[
a=CU^{-1}B,\qquad a\in R_n.
\]
Next write
\[
d-a=u+v,
\]
where $u$ is invertible and $v$ is an involution in $R_n$. Then $d$ can be represented as
\[
d=u+a+v.
\]
Therefore
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}U&B\\C&a+u\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}D&0\\0&v\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Clearly, the second matrix in the sum is a diagonal involution. We show that the first matrix is invertible. Introduce two invertible matrices $P$ and $Q$:
\[
P=
\begin{pmatrix}
I&0\\
-CU^{-1}&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q=
\begin{pmatrix}
U^{-1}&-U^{-1}Bu^{-1}\\
0&u^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here $I$ is the identity matrix of order $n-1$. Denote the first matrix in the sum by
\[
V=\begin{pmatrix}U&B\\C&a+u\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Computing the product $PVQ$, we obtain
\[
PVQ=
\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus the product is the identity matrix, and therefore $V$ is invertible.

Hence $M$ is the sum of an invertible matrix and an involution. Consequently, the formal matrix ring $K$ has the involution property.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Let \(F\) be a field of characteristic different from \(2\). Then \(F\) has the involution property.

Indeed, the elements \(1\) and \(-1\) are involutions. For any \(a\in F\), if \(a\neq 1\), then
\[
a=(a-1)+1,
\]
and \(a-1\) is invertible. If \(a=1\), then
\[
1=2+(-1),
\]
where \(2\) is invertible because \(\operatorname{char}F\neq 2\). Thus every element of \(F\) is a sum of an invertible element and an involution.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Consider the ring of upper triangular matrices
\[
K=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbb{F}_3 & \mathbb{F}_3\\
0 & \mathbb{F}_3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Since \(\mathbb{F}_3\) has the involution property, Proposition~6 implies that \(K\) also has the involution property.

For example,
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
0&2
\end{pmatrix}
\]
admits the decomposition
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first matrix is invertible, while the second matrix is an involution, since
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}^{2}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
over \(\mathbb{F}_3\).
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- counterexample-1: body_md -->
The field \(\mathbb{F}_2\) does not have the involution property.

Indeed, its only invertible element is \(1\), and its only involution is also \(1\). Hence the only element representable as the sum of an invertible element and an involution is
\[
1+1=0.
\]
Therefore \(1\in\mathbb{F}_2\) has no such representation.
<!-- end counterexample-1 -->
<!-- counterexample-2: body_md -->
The ring of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) does not have the involution property.

The only invertible elements of \(\mathbb{Z}\) are \(1\) and \(-1\), and these are also its only involutions. Consequently, the possible sums of an invertible element and an involution are only
\[
-2,\qquad 0,\qquad 2.
\]
In particular, the element \(1\) cannot be represented in the required form.
Therefore \(\mathbb{Z}\) does not have the involution property.

Consequently, by Proposition~6, the triangular matrix ring
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbb{Z}&\mathbb{Z}\\
0&\mathbb{Z}
\end{pmatrix}
\]
does not have the involution property either.
<!-- end counterexample-2 -->
